title: OWASP Top 10 Overview
summary: The OWASP Top 10 is a data-driven ranking of the most common web app risks, not an opinion list — and it's the floor for a security review, not the ceiling. This topic maps the list and how the rest of this group fills it in.

slides.markdown:
Ask any security engineer "where do I even start reviewing this app" and the answer is almost always the same: **the OWASP Top 10**. It's a ranked list of the ten most impactful web application risk categories, published by the nonprofit Open Worldwide Application Security Project and rebuilt roughly every 3-4 years from real breach and scan data.

It isn't a checklist you tick once and forget — it's a **floor**. Every topic in this Application Security group and the next one, Authentication & Authorization, maps onto one or more of its ten categories. Learn the map first; the rest of both groups fills in the mechanism.

What it doesn't do: rank every possible vulnerability, cover business-logic flaws specific to your app, or stay current between releases. Treat it as a floor, not a scorecard.

slides.sectionTitle: What it is and how it's compiled
slides.markdown:
The OWASP Top 10 is **not** a poll of what security experts find scary. Recent editions are built from two kinds of evidence:

- **Contributed data** — dozens of organizations submit anonymized vulnerability data from their own scanning and testing tools, covering hundreds of CWEs (Common Weakness Enumerations) across hundreds of thousands of applications.
- **An industry survey** — practitioners vote on categories they believe are under-represented in the data but that they see recurring in the field (this is how *Insecure Design* and *SSRF* entered the list before the data alone would have surfaced them).

OWASP then clusters related CWEs into ten named categories and orders them primarily by a mix of **incidence rate** and **exploitability/impact**, not just raw frequency. That's why a category can rank high even if it isn't the single most common CWE — a rarer but catastrophic weakness class outranks a common but low-impact one.

The result ships as a public, versioned document (2017, 2021, and so on) — free, vendor-neutral, and the shared vocabulary every pentest report and bug bounty program uses.

slides.sectionTitle: The current categories at a glance
slides.subTitle: 2021 edition
slides.markdown:
The 2021 list, in rank order:

1. **Broken Access Control** — users acting outside their intended permissions
2. **Cryptographic Failures** — weak, missing, or misused crypto exposing sensitive data
3. **Injection** — untrusted data interpreted as code (SQL, command, etc.)
4. **Insecure Design** — missing or ineffective security controls baked into the architecture itself
5. **Security Misconfiguration** — insecure defaults, verbose errors, unpatched software
6. **Vulnerable & Outdated Components** — using libraries or frameworks with known flaws
7. **Identification & Authentication Failures** — weak login, session, and credential handling
8. **Software & Data Integrity Failures** — trusting unsigned code, updates, or serialized data
9. **Security Logging & Monitoring Failures** — breaches going undetected for lack of visibility
10. **Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)** — tricking a server into making requests on the attacker's behalf

Notice #1 dethroned Injection, which had topped every prior list — access control bugs are now both more common and, thanks to modern scanning tools getting better at finding them, more visible in the data.

slides.sectionTitle: Where each category lives in a request
slides.markdown:
The ten categories aren't a random bag — they cluster around specific points in a request's journey through your system, and knowing the cluster tells you where to *look* during a review.

![OWASP Top 10 categories grouped by where they occur in a request's lifecycle: client, network, application, and data stages](assets/request-lifecycle-categories.svg)

The practical takeaway: Injection and Broken Access Control live almost entirely in your application code, so code review catches them. Security Misconfiguration and Vulnerable Components live in your infrastructure and dependency tree, so a code review alone will miss them — you need config audits and dependency scanning too. A checklist that only does one kind of review is guaranteed to miss a category.

slides.sectionTitle: A floor, not a complete program
slides.markdown:
| | OWASP Top 10 | A complete security program |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | Ten highest-impact web app categories | Every asset: infra, mobile, supply chain, physical, people |
| **Depth** | One category can hide dozens of distinct CWEs | Threat models specific to *your* architecture and data |
| **Cadence** | Refreshed every 3-4 years | Continuous — every release, every new integration |
| **Business logic** | Not covered — it's abuse-case, not weakness-class | Explicitly modeled per feature |
| **Use** | Minimum bar for any web app review | The actual risk register a security team owns |

The list is deliberately narrow so it stays memorable and universal. A team that stops at "we're not in the Top 10" has covered the ten most common categories of *known* weakness classes — and said nothing about whether their refund logic can be abused to issue infinite refunds, which is a business-logic flaw no CWE captures.

slides.sectionTitle: How this group splits from Authentication & Authorization
slides.markdown:
This group (Application Security) and the next one (Authentication & Authorization) between them cover most of the ten categories, split by concern rather than by category number:

- **This group** takes the *input-handling and output-handling* categories: Injection, XSS, CSRF, Security Misconfiguration, Broken Access Control's application-layer bugs (IDOR, missing checks), Insecure Deserialization, and SSRF.
- **Authentication & Authorization** takes the *identity* categories: Identification & Authentication Failures, and the authorization *design* patterns (RBAC, ABAC, OAuth2, OIDC) that Broken Access Control bugs violate.

The overlap is intentional, not sloppy: [Broken Access Control](broken-access-control) here covers the application-layer *bugs* (a missing ownership check on `/orders/1234`), while [Authorization Models](authorization-models) there covers the *design patterns* meant to prevent them. You need both — a well-designed RBAC system with a missing check on one route is still broken access control.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the ranking moves between editions
slides.subTitle: The numbers behind the list
slides.markdown:
The rank order isn't cosmetic — it tracks real shifts in how software gets built:

- **Injection fell from #1 (2017) to #3 (2021)** not because SQL injection got rarer in absolute terms, but because parameterized queries and ORMs became the default in most frameworks, shrinking the *proportion* of apps affected.
- **Broken Access Control rose to #1** partly because automated scanners got dramatically better at detecting IDOR and missing-authorization patterns, surfacing bugs that were always there but previously invisible in the data.
- **Insecure Design and SSRF are new-ish categories** added via the practitioner survey — before they existed as named categories, their underlying CWEs were scattered and under-counted.

The lesson for a candidate: don't memorize "#1 is always injection" — that was true in 2017 and false by 2021. Know the *categories* and be able to explain why any of them might move, because interviewers sometimes probe exactly this to check you understand the list is evidence-driven, not folklore.

The most common misuse of this list: treating absence from it as a clean bill of health.

Three ways that fails in practice:

- **Business-logic abuse** — a coupon system that lets you apply the same code twice isn't a CWE at all; it's a flaw in *your* rules, and no generic list will ever name it.
- **Category ≠ exhaustive CWE coverage** — "Cryptographic Failures" bundles dozens of distinct weaknesses (weak ciphers, missing encryption at rest, predictable tokens, bad randomness). Passing a scan for one doesn't mean you've addressed the category.
- **New and niche attack classes lag the list** — supply-chain attacks on build pipelines and AI-specific risks (prompt injection into an LLM feature) predate or sit outside the current ten entirely.

A scan report that says "0 OWASP Top 10 findings" is a floor cleared, not a ceiling reached. Say this explicitly in a review: "clean against the Top 10" and "secure" are different claims.

slides.sectionTitle: Using it as a working tool, not a poster
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
Junior use of the list: print it, tick boxes. Senior use: turn it into three concrete artifacts.

- **A review checklist mapped to your stack.** "Injection" becomes "every raw SQL string in `/services` gets grepped for string concatenation with request data" — a specific, runnable check, not a category name.
- **A threat-modeling prompt.** For each new feature, ask which of the ten categories it could newly expose. A feature that fetches a URL the user supplies is an SSRF question before it's anything else.
- **A common vocabulary with auditors and bug bounty researchers.** When a pentest report cites "A01:2021 – Broken Access Control," you should immediately know which of your own code patterns (missing ownership checks, client-side-only gating) it's pointing at without looking it up.

The list's real value to a staff engineer isn't the ranking — it's that it's a shared, battle-tested taxonomy for a conversation that would otherwise be ad hoc.

The rest of this group works through the input/output-handling half of the list in depth: [Security Misconfiguration & Logging Failures](security-misconfig-logging) first, since those are failures of *absence* rather than a specific exploit technique, then the exploit-driven categories — [Injection Attacks](injection-attacks), [Cross-Site Scripting](xss), [CSRF](csrf), [Broken Access Control](broken-access-control), and finally the advanced pair, Insecure Deserialization & SSRF.

Keep this topic's map in mind as you go: each one names which OWASP category it belongs to, and by the end of the group you'll be able to place any web app finding onto this list without hesitating.
